title: High-Stakes Environments
hook: When the stakes rise, attention narrows to the threat you expect, and the signal you need arrives from just outside that tunnel.
why:
The moments in which reading people matters most are the moments in which it is hardest to do. A man shouting in a public place. A disciplinary meeting that could end someone's job. A negotiation with a great deal of money on the table. A conversation with a teenager you think may be in trouble. In each, your body prepares for a threat, your attention tightens, and you feel more alert than ever. You are also, measurably, seeing less.

This chapter is about reading when it counts. It explains how high stakes narrow attention and point it at whatever you expect, and why a reading made under that narrowing can create the evidence it was looking for. Then it gives you the tools that people in dangerous professions rely on: the pre-brief and the premortem before the event, dividing the work of talking and watching, using your own body to bring a situation down, and the debrief afterwards. None of them make you braver or cleverer. They make you see a little more of the room.

teach.p:
In 1959 J. A. Easterbrook proposed what he called the cue-utilisation hypothesis. As emotional arousal rises, the range of cues a person uses shrinks. At first this helps: irrelevant details drop away and attention concentrates on the task. As arousal keeps rising, relevant cues at the edges start to drop away too, and performance falls. The beam of attention gets brighter and narrower at the same time.

Research on eyewitnesses gives the clearest picture of this. In 1987 Elizabeth Loftus, Geoffrey Loftus and Jane Messo tracked the eye movements of people watching a staged scene in a restaurant, in which a customer either handed a cashier a cheque or pointed a gun at her. When the gun was present, viewers fixated on it more often and for longer, and afterwards they were worse at identifying the man holding it. Later reviews have found the weapon-focus effect repeatedly. The threat drew the eyes, and the face, which was what a witness would later need, went less noticed.

Everyday high stakes do the same on a smaller scale. In an angry conversation you watch the other person's face and hands and lose the room around them. In a tense meeting you watch the person you fear and miss the colleague who has gone quiet. And because the narrowing comes with a feeling of heightened alertness, you are unlikely to notice that it is happening.

The first defence is simply to know this about yourself. When your heart rate rises and the situation seems to sharpen, assume that your field has shrunk. The signal you need is probably outside it.

Feeling alert is not the same as seeing widely. Under pressure, it usually means the opposite.
teach.disconfirm: If, after a tense situation, you can describe the edges of the room, who was there and what they were doing, as fully as after a calm one, your attention did not narrow much under that level of stress. Test it by writing such a description within an hour of your next tense moment.

teach.h: The threat you expect is the one you see.
teach.p:
Narrowing has a direction. Attention does not shrink towards the centre of the scene but towards whatever you already believe is the threat. That is what makes high-stakes reading so dangerous: the expectation you bring decides where the beam points, and anything outside it, including evidence against the expectation, goes unseen.

Investigators have a name for this when it goes wrong in criminal cases: tunnel vision. Keith Findley and Michael Scott, reviewing wrongful convictions in 2006, described how investigators who settled early on a suspect went on to notice and remember the evidence that fitted, explain away the evidence that did not, and stop looking for alternatives. None of this required bad faith. It is what attention does under pressure once it has a target.

The same pattern turns up in ordinary life. A manager who expects a resignation sees a resignation in every closed door and every long lunch. A father who suspects drugs sees them in every red eye and every mumbled answer, and misses the boy's grief over a friend who moved away. A man who expects a stranger to be dangerous watches his hands and misses that he is lost and frightened.

The remedy is to name the expectation before the stakes rise. Write down, or say to a colleague, what you expect to happen and what you expect this person to do. Then add a rival: the most likely innocent explanation for the same situation. Naming both will not stop your attention from narrowing. It gives the narrowed attention two targets instead of one, and that alone keeps more of the room in view.

Expectation is the hand on the torch. Decide where it points before the dark arrives.
teach.disconfirm: If you name an expectation and a rival before a high-stakes conversation and find that, afterwards, you noticed no more evidence for the rival than you would have otherwise, naming did not widen your attention. Try writing the rival with a specific behaviour to watch for.

teach.p:
The most serious danger of high-stakes reading is that it can create the behaviour it takes as proof. The clearest evidence comes from the study of police interrogation, and it is a warning for everyone else.

In 2003 Saul Kassin, Christine Goldstein and Kenneth Savitsky had students play interrogators questioning other students, some of whom had committed a mock theft and some of whom had not. Some interrogators were led to expect guilt. Those interrogators chose more questions that presumed guilt, pressed harder, and worked to get a confession. The suspects they questioned, including the innocent ones, became more defensive, and neutral observers listening to the tapes then judged those suspects more likely to be guilty. The expectation had produced its own evidence.

The real-world cost of this is documented. A 2010 review by Kassin and colleagues, written for the American Psychology-Law Society, set out the risk factors for false confessions, including long interrogations, presentation of false evidence, youth and intellectual disability, and noted that false confessions had featured in a substantial share of the cases later overturned by DNA evidence in the United States. Innocent people confess under pressure far more often than most people believe possible.

You are unlikely ever to interrogate anyone. But the pattern holds in every setting where one person questions another with something at stake: a disciplinary hearing, a parent confronting a teenager, a partner confronting a partner. If you go in having decided, your questions, your tone and your body will push the other person into defensiveness, and their defensiveness will look exactly like the guilt you expected.

Go in with a question, not a verdict, and let your questions be ones an innocent person could answer calmly.
teach.disconfirm: If, when you go into a hard conversation having decided in advance, the other person's behaviour looks no more defensive than when you go in open, presumption is not distorting your evidence in that setting. Your own reading of their defensiveness cannot settle it, so ask a neutral third person who was present.
teach.pullQuote: Their defensiveness will look exactly like the guilt you expected.

teach.p:
People in dangerous professions do much of their best reading before the event. Flight crews brief the approach before they fly it. Surgical teams pause before the first incision. Police and negotiators gather and talk through what they know. The point of a pre-brief is to decide in calm what attention will be too narrow to decide under pressure: what we expect, what would surprise us, and who will watch for what.

One of the most useful additions to a pre-brief is the premortem, which the psychologist Gary Klein described in 2007. Instead of asking what could go wrong, which invites optimism, you imagine that the event has already happened and gone badly, and ask why. The idea draws on earlier work by Deborah Mitchell, Jay Russo and Nancy Pennington, who found in 1989 that imagining an outcome as already certain helped people come up with more reasons for it than imagining it as merely possible.

A personal premortem for a hard conversation takes five minutes. *It is an hour from now and the conversation went badly. What happened?* Write every reason you can think of. Most will be about you: you lost your temper, you assumed, you missed something. Then turn each reason into a plan, and each missed thing into something to watch for. If one reason is *I didn't notice he was frightened*, then fear goes on your list of rivals, with the signs you would expect to see.

Keep the pre-brief short enough to remember. Three lines are enough: what I expect, the rival I will watch for, and the one thing I must not do.

The failures you imagine in advance are the ones you have a chance of seeing in time.
teach.disconfirm: If your premortems for hard conversations consistently fail to name the thing that actually went wrong, they are not drawing on your real patterns. Look back through your journal for the commonest causes of your past failures and start the next premortem with those.

teach.h: Divide the talking from the watching.
teach.p:
It is very hard to talk and watch at the same time when the stakes are high. Talking under pressure takes most of your attention: choosing words, managing your voice, holding the thread. Watching takes the rest. For this reason, professions that work under pressure often split the two jobs between different people.

In aviation, one pilot flies and the other monitors, calling out what the flying pilot may have missed. In crisis negotiation teams, a primary negotiator talks while a second listens to every word, watches the whole situation and passes notes. In anaesthesia, a model called crisis resource management, developed by David Gaba and colleagues in the 1990s, teaches that in an emergency one person should stand back and keep the overview rather than join the hands-on work.

You can do the same in ordinary high-stakes situations. In a difficult negotiation or a hard meeting, agree with a colleague beforehand who will talk and who will watch, what the watcher is looking for, and a discreet way of passing on what they see. At a difficult medical appointment, take a friend whose only job is to listen and to notice. In a tense public situation at work, one person speaks and another watches the crowd and the person's hands.

The watcher's notes are also the best material for a debrief, because they come from someone whose attention was not narrowed by having to perform.

When you have to do both jobs alone, do them in turns. Talk, then pause and look round deliberately, then talk again. The pause costs a second, and it is when you are most likely to see what you have missed.
teach.disconfirm: If the person who watches sees nothing that the person talking missed, over several high-stakes situations, either the talker's attention is unusually wide or the watcher has not been told what to watch for. Brief the watcher more specifically before deciding the split is unnecessary.

teach.h: Use your own body to bring it down.
teach.p:
In a tense encounter, the one body you can control is your own, and it is a large part of what the other person is reading. Bodies tend to answer each other. Raised voices draw raised voices, squared shoulders draw squared shoulders, and fast movement draws fast movement. De-escalation begins by refusing to join that loop.

The physical elements are simple and run against instinct. Stand at an angle rather than squarely, which is less confrontational and gives both of you room. Keep your hands visible, open and still, and away from your face and pockets. Keep your distance, or step back if the other person steps forward. Lower your voice and slow your speech, since people under stress tend to match the pace and volume around them. Use fewer words. If you can, sit down, or invite the other person to sit. And breathe out slowly before you speak, which steadies your own voice.

There is growing evidence that training people in this way of behaving works. In 2022 Robin Engel and colleagues evaluated a de-escalation training programme in the police department of Louisville, Kentucky, and found that after the training, use of force fell by more than a quarter, injuries to members of the public by about a quarter, and injuries to officers by about a third.

These are not tricks for winning. They are ways of making a situation less dangerous for everyone in it, including the person who is frightening you. They do not replace your judgment about safety. If you see a weapon, or the situation is getting worse despite your efforts, your job is to get yourself and others to safety and call for help.

Calm is easiest to lend when you have actually got some. Check your own breath first.
teach.disconfirm: If, in tense encounters you are part of, slowing down, lowering your voice and angling your body make no difference to how quickly the other person calms, compared with your usual manner, these elements are not what matters in your setting. Keep a short record of a dozen such encounters before deciding.

teach.p:
The United States Army developed the after-action review as a way of learning from exercises and operations, and versions of it are now used in hospitals, fire services and companies. It asks four questions. What was supposed to happen? What actually happened? Why was there a difference? What will we do differently next time?

Debriefs work. In 2013 Scott Tannenbaum and Christopher Cerasoli combined the evidence from dozens of studies and found that teams and individuals who debriefed improved their performance by about a quarter on average, compared with those who did not. The effect held for real teams as well as in simulations, and it did not depend on expensive equipment.

For a reader, the debrief should include the reading itself. What did I expect, and where was my attention? Which signals did I use? What was happening outside my focus that I missed, and who saw it? Did my questions or my body shape the behaviour I saw? Were the readings I acted on right, and how do I know?

Do it within hours, while memory is still close to the event, for the reasons the journal chapter set out. Do it when things went well too. A high-stakes situation that went well is the one you are most likely to explain with a flattering story, and the one where the luck you had is easiest to mistake for skill.

And keep it blameless. A debrief that looks for someone to blame teaches everyone to hide what they missed, which is exactly the information the debrief exists to find.
teach.disconfirm: If your debriefs over several months produce no changes in how you handle high-stakes situations, or the same misses keep recurring, the debriefs are not reaching the cause. Ask someone who was present to run the next one with you, and to ask the fourth question.

caseStudy:
Kwame, forty-seven, is a duty manager at a busy railway station. On a Friday evening a man starts shouting at a ticket barrier, slamming his palm on the glass. Two of Kwame's staff begin to move towards him, and the people nearby step back.

Kwame stops his colleague Ade and gives a ten-second pre-brief. *I'll talk. You watch his hands and the people around him. If you see anything I should know, touch your ear.* He names his expectation to himself, a fight, and a rival, someone in trouble.

He approaches at an angle, stops a couple of metres away, keeps his hands open at his sides, and speaks more quietly than the man is shouting. *I'm Kwame, I run the station tonight. Tell me what's happened.* The man shouts that the barrier will not take his ticket. Kwame is watching the man's hands, which are still slapping the glass. Ade touches his ear.

Kwame glances where Ade is looking. By a pillar stands a girl of about eight with a small rucksack, crying. The man keeps glancing at her. Kwame had not seen her at all. *Is she with you?* he asks. The man's shoulders drop. She is his daughter. He is meant to hand her over to her mother at the other end of the line, the custody arrangement is strict, and his ticket is for the wrong day.

Kwame lets them through and phones ahead to the other station. The whole thing takes six minutes.

Afterwards he and Ade run a short debrief in the office. What did they expect? A fight. What happened? A frightened father. What did Kwame miss? The girl, because his attention had narrowed to the hands. What will they do next time? Exactly the same split, because the watcher saw what the talker could not.
observe: The next time your heart rate rises in a conversation, notice afterwards how much of the room you can still describe, and what you cannot.
Before a conversation that matters to you, write down what you expect the other person to do, so that you can compare it with what happens.
In a tense public moment you witness, notice where most people's eyes go, and what is happening just outside that point.

drills.name: Personal Premortem
steps: Choose a hard conversation you expect to have in the next fortnight.
Write at the top: it is an hour afterwards and the conversation went badly. Then list every reason you can think of.
Mark the reasons that are about you rather than the other person.
Turn each marked reason into a plan, and each thing you might miss into a sign to watch for.
Compress the result to three lines: what you expect, the rival you will watch for, and the one thing you must not do.
variations: Run the premortem for a conversation that has already happened, and compare your list with what actually went wrong.
Ask a trusted friend to add three reasons to your list that you did not think of, without seeing your three lines first.
Run a premortem for a conversation you expect to go well, and see whether it finds anything you would otherwise have missed.

drills.name: Edge Check
steps: Choose a moderately tense situation you will be in this week, such as a difficult meeting or a crowded journey.
At its tensest moment, breathe out slowly and look deliberately at the edges of the room or space.
Silently name three things you see at the edges.
Within an hour, write down everything you can remember about the edges of the scene.
Compare it with a similar note from a calm situation, and record the difference.
variations: Repeat the drill in a crowded place, such as a busy station, and see how much of the edges you can name while moving.
Do the edge check at the start of a tense meeting as well as at its tensest moment, and compare what you saw each time.
Ask a colleague who was present to write down what they noticed at the edges, and compare it with your own note.

drills.name: Divide the Watch
steps: Before a meeting or negotiation that matters, agree with a colleague who will talk and who will watch.
Tell the watcher two specific things to look for, and agree a discreet signal.
During the meeting, the talker pauses at least once to check for the signal.
Afterwards, the watcher reports what they saw that the talker missed.
Swap roles at the next suitable meeting and compare what each of you noticed.
variations: Try the split on a recorded interview first, with one of you watching only the interviewer and the other only the guest.
Change what the watcher looks for at each meeting, and record which brief produced the most useful report.
Agree a second signal that means something urgent, and practise both signals before a meeting where they might be needed.

drills.name: De-escalation Rehearsal
steps: With a friend, agree a stop word and a short scenario in which they play someone angry about something reasonable.
Run it for two minutes while you practise standing at an angle, hands open and still, voice low and slow, and few words.
Ask your friend which of your behaviours made them calmer and which made them angrier.
Run it again with your friend raising the intensity slightly.
Write down the one physical habit that was hardest to hold, and practise it alone for five minutes.
variations: Rehearse the scenario sitting down, as you might at a desk or counter, and notice which elements are harder to use from a chair.
Rehearse leaving: at a pre-agreed moment, say your prepared sentence and step away, and practise it until it feels natural.
Record the rehearsal on your phone and watch it back with the sound off, noting every movement that might read as a challenge.

drills.name: After-Action Review
steps: Within six hours of any high-stakes conversation or situation, open your journal.
Answer in writing: what was supposed to happen, and what actually happened.
Answer: why was there a difference, including where your attention was and what you missed.
Note whether your questions or your body may have shaped the behaviour you saw.
Write one specific thing you will do differently next time.
variations: Run the review for a high-stakes situation that went well, and look for any luck you might otherwise have called skill.
Ask someone who was present to answer the four questions separately, then compare your answers with theirs.
Keep a running list of the one thing you will do differently from each review, and read it before the next hard conversation.

quiz.q: When the stakes rise and you feel highly alert, do you notice more of what is going on?
options: Yes, because adrenaline sharpens every one of the senses at the same moment
No, because attention narrows onto the expected threat and drops the edges
Only if you have been through military or police training beforehand
Yes, as long as you keep your eyes moving steadily around the room
quiz.explain: Rising arousal narrows the range of cues you use, and it narrows towards whatever you expect. The feeling of alertness hides the narrowing, so assume your field has shrunk and look deliberately at the edges.

quiz.q: In studies of weapon focus, what happened to witnesses when a weapon was visible?
options: They looked at the weapon more and identified the person less well
They remembered every detail of the scene more clearly than usual
They remembered the face better, since it was linked to the threat
They could not later say whether a weapon had been there at all
quiz.explain: The threat drew their eyes, and the face that a witness would later need was noticed less. It is a precise example of attention narrowing towards the expected threat and dropping what lies outside it.

quiz.q: In Kassin, Goldstein and Savitsky's study, what happened when student interrogators were led to expect guilt?
options: They asked more neutral questions so as to avoid showing any bias
They became more accurate at picking out the guilty suspects
They behaved no differently from interrogators expecting innocence
They pressed harder, and their suspects then sounded more guilty
quiz.explain: Expecting guilt changed their questions and their pressure, which made suspects, including innocent ones, more defensive. Observers then judged those suspects more likely to be guilty, so the expectation produced its own evidence.

quiz.q: You are going into a disciplinary meeting convinced that an employee lied about his hours. What fits this chapter?
options: Watch him closely for any of the signs that people show when lying
Ask pointed questions designed to put pressure on him to admit it
Run a premortem, write a rival explanation, and ask open questions
Bring a colleague along with you to confirm what you both see
quiz.explain: Going in with a verdict will shape your questions and his defensiveness, which will then look like proof. A premortem and a named rival widen your attention, and open questions give an innocent explanation a fair chance to emerge.

quiz.q: What does a premortem ask you to do?
options: Review a failure after the event with everyone who took part in it
Imagine the plan has already failed and work out why
List all the strengths of a plan before presenting it to others
Ask an outside expert to predict whether the plan will succeed
quiz.explain: Imagining the failure as already certain makes it easier to come up with reasons for it than asking what might go wrong. For a hard conversation, the reasons usually point to what you might miss or do.

quiz.q: At a station, a man is shouting at a ticket barrier and two colleagues are moving towards him. What fits this chapter?
options: Approach him squarely, hold his eye, and tell him firmly and clearly to calm down
Keep well back from him and wait for the police to arrive, whatever happens next
Agree who talks and who watches, then approach at an angle, hands open, voice low
Gather several colleagues around him so that he can see he is outnumbered
quiz.explain: Splitting talking from watching keeps someone's attention wide, and an angled stance, open hands and a lower voice refuse to join the escalation. If you see a weapon or things get worse, get to safety and call for help.

quiz.q: What did Findley and Scott describe in 2006 about investigators who settled early on a suspect in cases that ended in wrongful convictions?
options: That they deliberately invented evidence against suspects they disliked, knowing that it was false
That they were careless, and simply failed to collect the evidence that would eventually have cleared the suspect
That they were usually right, and the convictions were overturned on technical points of procedure
That they noticed the evidence that fitted, explained away the rest and stopped looking, without bad faith
quiz.explain: Tunnel vision does not require bad faith. It is what attention does under pressure once it has a target, which is why naming a rival before the stakes rise matters so much.

quiz.q: What did Tannenbaum and Cerasoli find in 2013 when they combined studies of debriefs?
options: That debriefs made no measurable difference to performance, though most people said that they enjoyed them
That teams and individuals who debriefed improved their performance by about a quarter on average
That debriefs helped only in simulations, and made no difference to real teams doing real work
That debriefs worked only when they were run by outside experts with expensive video equipment
quiz.explain: The improvement held for real teams as well as in simulations, and did not depend on expensive equipment. A short, blameless review within hours of an event is one of the cheapest ways to get better at high-stakes work.

quiz.q: Someone says de-escalation training is soft and makes officers less safe. What did Engel and colleagues find in Louisville in 2022?
options: That injuries to officers rose sharply, because the training made them slower to protect themselves
That the training changed nothing, since use of force and injuries stayed exactly where they had been
That use of force fell by more than a quarter, and injuries to officers fell by about a third
That the training was abandoned after a few weeks, before anyone could measure what it had done
quiz.explain: After the training, use of force fell by more than a quarter, injuries to members of the public by about a quarter, and injuries to officers by about a third. Lowering the temperature made the situations safer for everyone in them, including the people trained.

reflection.prompt: Describe one specific high-stakes conversation or situation from the past year, at work, at home or in public, in which you later realised you had missed something important. What did you expect going in, and where was your attention? What was happening outside that focus? Which of the tools in this chapter, a premortem, a second pair of eyes, your own body or a debrief, would most likely have caught it, and how would you use it next time?
reflection.guidance: Choose a situation where something was genuinely at stake for you, because that is when narrowing happens. Most people find that what they missed was not hidden. It was in plain view, outside the place their expectation had pointed their attention. Name the expectation as precisely as you can, since that is what you will need to name in advance next time.

failureMode: The first failure is to trust the feeling of alertness, believing that because you feel sharp, you are seeing everything. The second is to go into a hard conversation with a verdict, so that your questions and your body produce the defensiveness you then read as proof. The third is to use the elements of de-escalation as a technique for winning rather than for reducing danger, which people sense quickly and which tends to make things worse. The fourth is to skip the debrief, either because the situation went well and you would rather keep the flattering story, or because it went badly and you would rather not look. The last is heroics: staying to read a situation that has become dangerous, when the right action was to leave and call for help.

moreCases.title: The mother who went in with a verdict
moreCases.scene:
Lisa, forty-six, has been worried about her son Jamie, sixteen, for a month. He has been staying in his room, keeping his phone face down, snapping at his sister, and twice she has heard him up at three in the morning. On Tuesday she finds that he has deleted the messages app from the family tablet he usually uses. A friend at work, whose nephew got into trouble, says it sounds like drugs.

That evening Lisa waits for Jamie in the kitchen. When he comes in she says, *I know what's going on. I want the truth.* Jamie stops in the doorway. His face goes red, he crosses his arms, and he says he does not know what she is talking about. Lisa asks who he is buying from. Jamie says she is mad. Lisa asks why, if he has nothing to hide, he has deleted his messages. Jamie shouts that she never trusts him, goes upstairs and slams the door.

Lisa sits at the table shaking, now more certain than before. An innocent boy, she thinks, would not have reacted like that.

Two weeks later Jamie's form tutor rings. Another pupil has reported that a group from Jamie's year has been sending him abusive messages every night for over a month, and that he had deleted the app so that his little sister would not see them.

Jamie's sister, eleven, had heard everything from the landing. She did not come down to dinner.
moreCases.misread:
Lisa read Jamie's red face, crossed arms and anger as the defensiveness of guilt. She had gone in with a verdict, and her questions presumed it, which pushed him into exactly the defensiveness she then took as proof.

She also read her friend's story about a nephew as evidence about her own son, which gave her expectation a borrowed certainty before she had spoken to him.
moreCases.betterRead:
This is the Kassin, Goldstein and Savitsky pattern in a kitchen. Interrogators who expected guilt asked guilt-presuming questions, pressed harder, and produced defensive behaviour in innocent people, which observers then read as guilt. A boy accused of something he has not done reacts much as a guilty one would. A premortem would have helped: *It is an hour from now and the conversation went badly. Why?* Because I accused him, because I was wrong, because he was hiding something else. The better opening was a question an innocent person could answer calmly: *You've seemed really unhappy lately, and I'm worried. Is something going on?*

When Lisa finally asked that question, after the form tutor's call, Jamie cried, and told her everything. The school dealt with the group, and Lisa apologised for the kitchen.

The question would not have stopped Jamie being upset. It would have left room for the true answer, instead of a fight about the wrong one.

moreCases.title: The store detective's tunnel
moreCases.scene:
Gary, fifty, has worked as a store detective in a large department store for twelve years. On a Saturday afternoon two teenage boys in hooded tops come into the electronics section, and Gary's attention locks on. He has seen boys like this steal headphones before. He follows them at a distance, watching their hands and their pockets as they pick up boxes, put them down and laugh at something on a phone.

For twenty minutes he watches nothing else. The boys handle several boxes and put each one back. Gary is certain they are waiting for their moment.

At the end of the afternoon the stock count shows that six pairs of expensive headphones have gone from the very display Gary was standing near. The store's cameras show a well-dressed man in his forties, carrying a large shopping bag from another shop, filling it from the display while Gary stood five metres away, facing the other direction, watching the boys.

The boys left without buying anything. On the camera footage, one of them can be seen asking an assistant about a pair of headphones, checking the price on his phone and leaving with his friend.

Gary's report for the afternoon describes the boys in detail, with times and movements, and does not mention the man at all.

Gary is good at his job. In twelve years he has caught more shoplifters than anyone else in the store, which is part of why he trusts the feeling.
moreCases.misread:
Gary read two teenagers in hoods as thieves before they had done anything, and his attention narrowed to the threat he expected. Everything outside that beam, including the actual theft happening beside him, went unseen.

He also read his own long experience as protection against error, when it was what gave the expectation its force.

And he read the boys putting every box back as patience, the kind of detail that would have counted against his reading if he had been looking for one.
moreCases.betterRead:
Narrowing has a direction: towards whatever you already believe is the threat. Findley and Scott described the same pattern in criminal investigations, and Gary's afternoon is the same thing at small scale. He noticed every movement that fitted, explained away the boys putting everything back as waiting, and stopped looking anywhere else. Naming the expectation and a rival would have given his attention two targets instead of one, and the store's practice changed after that afternoon. Detectives now work in pairs on busy days, one following any suspicion and the other keeping the wider floor in view.

Gary also started writing down, at the start of each shift, one expectation he held and one rival, which he found embarrassing at first and useful within a week.

When the store manager asked him what had happened, Gary said, to his credit, that he had been watching the wrong people for the wrong reasons.

moreCases.title: The founder who negotiated alone
moreCases.scene:
Rebecca, forty-one, is selling the software company she started ten years ago. The first full negotiating session with the buyer is in a hotel meeting room: Rebecca on one side, and on the other the buyer's chief executive, its finance director and a lawyer. Her co-founder, Ian, offered to come, but Rebecca decided that she knows the numbers best and that two people on her side might look nervous.

For three hours she talks almost without a break: answering questions, defending the valuation, explaining the growth figures. She watches the chief executive, who is friendly and seems keen. She leaves feeling that the session went well and that a deal is close.

The buyer's next offer is twenty percent lower than the one discussed in the room. Their email cites concerns about customer contracts that Rebecca does not remember being raised. When she rings the chief executive, he says the finance director had raised them several times.

Rebecca goes back through her notes. She has three pages on what the chief executive said and almost nothing on the finance director, who, she now remembers vaguely, sat slightly apart and spoke quietly.

Ian had suggested a simple split before the session, him watching and her talking, and she had said it was not that kind of meeting.

In the taxi afterwards she rings Ian and tells him it could not have gone better.
moreCases.misread:
Rebecca read the session through the person she was talking to, and read his friendliness as the buyer's position. Talking for three hours under high stakes left her with no attention for the quieter person who was raising the concerns that would shape the offer.

She also read her own fluency in the room, three hours of confident answers, as a sign that the session was going her way.
moreCases.betterRead:
It is very hard to talk and watch at the same time when the stakes are high, which is why professions that work under pressure split the two jobs. For the next session Rebecca brought Ian, and they agreed in advance who would talk and who would watch: Ian would watch the finance director and the lawyer, and touch his pen when either reacted to something Rebecca said. Twice in the first hour he touched it, both times at questions about contract terms. Rebecca stopped and asked the finance director directly what concerned her. They spent an hour on it, and the final price came back most of the way.

Rebecca said afterwards that the hardest part was letting Ian sit there and say nothing, which felt like wasting him. It was the most useful thing he did all year.

moreCases.title: The pharmacist who stepped back
moreCases.scene:
Siobhan, thirty-three, runs a small community pharmacy. Late one afternoon a man in his thirties comes to the counter for a prescription that has not yet arrived from the surgery. He is angry and loud from the start. Siobhan does what she has practised: she stands at an angle, keeps her hands open and still on the counter, lowers her voice, and says she can see this is a real problem and she will ring the surgery now.

For a minute it seems to help. Then the man's voice rises again. He starts to swear, leans across the counter, and sweeps a display of leaflets onto the floor. Siobhan's assistant, Joy, nineteen, is standing behind him by the shelves, frozen.

Siobhan feels a strong pull to keep trying: to find the sentence that will bring him down, to stay calm and in control, to not be the pharmacist who called the police over a prescription.

Instead she says, steadily, *I'm going to step into the back and ring the surgery,* and she signals to Joy to come round the counter. They go into the back room together and Siobhan locks the door and calls the police. The man leaves before they arrive.

Afterwards, in the back room, Siobhan's hands shake so much that she has to put the phone on the desk to dial.
moreCases.misread:
Siobhan's first impulse read the situation as one she should still be able to manage with the right words. The pull to stay and keep trying was a reading of her role, not of the danger, which was rising despite everything she had done.

Joy read her own freezing, afterwards, as a sign that she was no good at the job, which was not true and needed saying.
moreCases.betterRead:
The elements of de-escalation are ways of making a situation less dangerous for everyone, not techniques for winning. They do not replace judgment about safety, and when a situation is getting worse despite your efforts, the right action is to get yourself and others to safety and call for help. Siobhan read the escalation correctly: a voice rising again after calming, physical damage, a colleague in the line of it. Leaving was the reading, not a failure of it. The debrief the next morning was blameless. Joy said she had frozen because she did not know what she was meant to do, and they agreed a simple plan for next time: a word that means *go to the back now*.

Siobhan also reported the incident to her area manager and asked for de-escalation training for the whole team, including what to do when it does not work.

Joy said, months later, that the most useful thing Siobhan had told her was that leaving is part of the job.

workedReading.title: A difficult family meeting, start to finish
workedReading.scene:
Helen, fifty-two, manages a care home. Mrs Reid, eighty-eight, one of the residents, fell in her room on Sunday night and was taken to hospital with a broken wrist. Her son, Daniel, has demanded a meeting, and his email is furious: he says the home is understaffed and negligent, and that he is making a formal complaint. The meeting is on Wednesday. Daniel will come with his sister, Claire, whom Helen has met once. Helen has decided to run the whole sequence from this chapter: a premortem, a pre-brief, a divided watch, and an after-action review. Her deputy, Sunita, forty, will sit in.

She has also read Mrs Reid's care notes for the past six months, so that she knows the facts before she has to think under pressure.

Helen knows her own habit under pressure, which is to explain and defend, and she has planned the meeting around it.

steps.label: Run the premortem
steps.text:
On Tuesday afternoon Helen writes at the top of a page: *It is Wednesday at four and the meeting went badly. Why?* She lists every reason she can think of. I got defensive about staffing. I talked over Daniel. I treated it as a complaint to manage rather than a frightened son. I missed what Claire thought. I promised something I cannot deliver. I did not find out what they actually want. Then she marks the reasons that are about her. All but one are.

The one reason that is not about her is Daniel's anger. She notes that it is the only one she cannot change, and the one she would have spent most time on if she had not done the exercise.

steps.label: Three-line pre-brief
steps.text:
She compresses the premortem into three lines and learns them. *I expect: anger at me, and a demand for someone to be blamed. The rival I'll watch for: fear and guilt, about their mother and about not visiting. The one thing I must not do: defend the staffing before I have heard them out.* She also writes down what she knows about the fall, in order, so that she does not have to work it out under pressure.

She also decides what she can and cannot offer, so that she will not promise anything in the room that she has not thought through.

steps.label: Brief the watcher
steps.text:
On Wednesday morning she briefs Sunita. *I'll talk. You watch Claire, and Daniel's hands. If either of them reacts strongly to something I say, or if Claire looks as if she wants to speak, put your pen down on the table.* She also asks Sunita to note anything she sees outside what Helen is attending to, and to say nothing in the meeting unless Helen asks her a direct question.

She also tells Sunita that if the meeting becomes abusive, she will end it, and that Sunita should take Claire out first if that happens.

Sunita asks what she should do if she sees something Helen ought to know urgently. They agree that she will say Helen's name, which in that room will be enough.

steps.label: Open with a question
steps.text:
When they arrive, Helen sits at the corner of the table rather than across it, and before saying anything about the fall, she asks Daniel how his mother is. He starts angry, as she expected: the staffing, the negligence, the complaint. Helen listens without interrupting, keeps her voice low and slow, and says she can see how frightening Sunday night must have been. Daniel's voice drops a little. Then he says, quietly, that he only found out at seven the next morning.

That sentence changes the meeting. The anger, Helen realises, is partly about the hours he did not know, lying awake afterwards.

Helen lets the silence after that sentence sit. She does not fill it with an explanation, which is what she would usually do.

steps.label: The signal from the watcher
steps.text:
At that point Sunita puts her pen down. Helen glances at Claire, whom she had barely looked at. Claire is holding a folder on her lap and has been nodding at every point about staffing. Helen asks her directly: *Claire, is there something you'd like to add?* Claire opens the folder. It holds a list, dated over six months, of small things she has noticed on visits: a call bell out of reach, a cold cup of tea, her mother's glasses left on the windowsill. She had never raised them because she did not want to make a fuss.

Helen thanks Claire, says she should have been told about these things directly, and asks whether she may take a copy of the list.

steps.label: After-action: four questions
steps.text:
That afternoon Helen and Sunita run the review. What was supposed to happen? A meeting that heard the family out and agreed next steps. What happened? Mostly that, with a written list of concerns that changed the meeting. Why the difference? Helen's attention had narrowed to Daniel, the person she expected to be the problem. Sunita saw Claire. What will they do differently? Use the same split in every family meeting about an incident, and ask families for written concerns at every review.

They also note the thing Helen nearly did: defend the staffing levels in her first answer. The pre-brief line stopped her.

steps.label: What changed afterwards
steps.text:
Helen also writes down the part of the review that was about her own reading. She had expected anger and seen it; the rival she had named, fear and guilt, was also there, in Daniel's dropped voice when he mentioned seven in the morning. The family's complaint was withdrawn a month later, after the home changed its night-time procedure for informing families. Claire now emails Helen directly whenever she notices something.

She also shares the review, without names, with the other managers in her group, so that the split becomes standard practice.

Sunita's note from the meeting has one line Helen had not seen: Daniel touched his mother's photograph on the wall as he left.

moreFailures.title: Running a premortem only on the other person
moreFailures.body:
A premortem is easy to do badly. Asked why a hard conversation went wrong, most people list the other person's failings: he lost his temper, she lied, they would not listen. Those reasons may be true, but they give you nothing to do, and they confirm the expectation you went in with. The useful reasons are the ones about you: I assumed, I talked too much, I missed what was happening at the edges, I defended myself before I had heard them out. Mark those, and turn each into a plan. If your list contains no reasons about yourself, do it again and force yourself to write three. The premortem's power comes from imagining the failure as certain, and the failure you can most affect is your own. It is also the one your narrowed attention will be least able to see on the day.

A useful check is to show your list to someone who knows you and ask which reason they think is most likely. It is usually one you wrote last, or one you did not write at all.

moreFailures.title: A watcher with no brief
moreFailures.body:
Bringing a colleague to a hard meeting helps only if they know what their job is. A watcher with no brief tends to watch whatever you are watching, usually the person who is talking, and so sees the same narrow slice you do. Or they join in, adding a second voice and taking their own attention away from watching. Or they see something important and have no way of telling you. Before the meeting, tell the watcher specifically whom or what to watch, which may be a quiet person, someone's hands or the door. Agree a discreet signal and a moment when you will check for it. Agree too whether they may speak, and when. A brief takes two minutes and turns a second person in the room from company into a second pair of eyes.

The watcher's notes are also the best material for the debrief, but only if the watcher knew what to look for.

When you are the watcher, resist the urge to help by joining in. Your silence is what makes your attention available.

moreFailures.title: Telling someone to calm down
moreFailures.body:
Almost everyone who is angry or frightened has been told to calm down, and almost nobody has calmed down because of it. The phrase tells the person that their reaction is the problem, and that you are in charge of how they feel. It tends to raise the temperature rather than lower it. The same is true of a soothing, sing-song voice, which people under stress hear as condescension. De-escalation is mostly something you do with your own body and voice, not something you instruct the other person to do. Lower your own voice rather than asking them to lower theirs. Slow your own speech. Acknowledge the problem plainly: *I can see this has gone badly wrong for you.* Calm spreads when it is shown, not when it is demanded.

If you notice yourself about to say the phrase, take a breath and say what you can see instead.

The same goes for *there's no need to shout*, *let's all be reasonable* and *I understand how you feel* said before you have heard them. Each tells the person how to feel, rather than showing them that you have listened.

moreFailures.title: Treating the debrief as a verdict on a person
moreFailures.body:
After a high-stakes situation goes badly, a debrief can easily turn into a hunt for whoever made the mistake. The person who froze, the one who said the wrong thing, the one who did not spot the danger: each becomes the explanation, and everyone else relaxes. A debrief run that way teaches people to hide what they missed, which is exactly the information it exists to find. Keep the four questions about the situation and the process, not the person: where was attention, what was outside it, what would have helped us see it. When someone did freeze or miss something, the useful question is what would have made it easier to do otherwise, such as a clearer plan, a signal or practice. Siobhan's debrief with Joy produced a code word, not a reprimand.

A blameless debrief is not one in which nothing is anyone's fault. It is one in which the aim is learning rather than punishment, so that people tell the truth about what they missed.

Leaders can make this easier by going first: saying what they missed, plainly, at the start of the review.

questions.q: What should I do if I am alone with someone who is getting angrier, and nobody is around to help?
questions.a:
Put safety first. Keep a clear route to the door, and do not stand between the other person and their own way out either, since someone who feels trapped is more dangerous. Keep your distance, or step back if they step forward. Use few words, a low voice and open, still hands, as the chapter describes. Do not argue the point, and do not try to win. If the situation is getting worse despite your efforts, leave, and call the emergency services as soon as you are safe. Your belongings, your shop's stock and your pride do not matter. A reading that it is time to go is a good reading, and acting on it early is better than acting on it late.

Afterwards, write down what happened and report it if it took place at work. Being frightened by someone is worth reporting even when nobody was hurt.

If you work somewhere that this could happen, such as a shop, a reception or a clinic, ask your employer what the plan is before you need it: where to go, how to call for help, and who else should know.

questions.q: How can I avoid going in with a verdict when the evidence really does look bad?
questions.a:
Hold the evidence, but do not open with it. Start by asking for the other person's account, with a question an innocent person could answer calmly: *Can you talk me through what happened on Thursday?* Listen to the whole answer before you mention what you know. Then put your evidence plainly and ask about it, rather than presenting it as a trap. Before the conversation, run a premortem with one specific question: *If I turn out to be wrong about this, what would the true story be?* Writing that story down gives your attention a second target. The evidence may still turn out to mean what you thought. But you will have heard the alternative, and the person will have had a fair chance to give it.

It also helps to have someone else look at the evidence before the conversation, someone with no stake in it, and ask them what else it could mean.

And remember that being wrong in private, before the conversation, costs nothing, while being wrong in the room can cost the other person a great deal.

questions.q: Is it ever right to confront someone directly about something serious, such as a worry that they might harm themselves?
questions.a:
Asking directly is not the same as confronting. If you are worried that someone may be thinking about suicide, the right thing is to ask them, calmly and plainly: *Are you thinking about killing yourself?* Asking does not put the idea in someone's head, and it often brings relief. Listen without arguing or panicking, stay with them if they are at risk, and help them connect with support, such as a GP, a crisis line or, if they are in immediate danger, the emergency services. This app's crisis resources list where to turn, and chapter 2.13 covers this in depth. What this chapter warns against is going in with a verdict about someone's behaviour. Going in with care and a direct question is the opposite.

If the person is a child or a vulnerable adult and you are worried about their safety, also follow your workplace's safeguarding route and report to the designated lead, rather than investigating yourself.

If you are not sure what to say, saying that you are worried and asking how they are is already a good start.

questions.q: How do I run a debrief when I was on my own and there was nobody to do it with?
questions.a:
Use your journal and the four questions, in writing, within a few hours. What was supposed to happen? What actually happened? Why was there a difference? What will I do differently next time? Add the reader's questions: where was my attention, what was outside it, did my own questions or body shape what I saw? Writing forces more honesty than thinking, because a vague answer looks vague on the page. It also helps to tell one trusted person the story briefly, and ask them what they would have noticed. If the situation was frightening, write the facts first and the feelings after, and be kind to yourself in both. A solo debrief is less complete than a shared one, and far better than none.

Over time, a series of solo reviews will show you patterns in where your attention goes under pressure, which is the most useful thing a debrief can teach.

questions.q: Do the de-escalation elements work on the phone or on a video call?
questions.a:
Partly. On the phone, your voice is the whole of your body, so the voice elements matter even more: lower, slower, fewer words, and a slow breath out before you speak. Silence is harder to read on a phone, so acknowledge what you hear more explicitly than you would in person. On a video call, open and still hands help if they are in view, and sitting back slightly from the camera looks less confrontational than leaning in. Dividing the talking from the watching still works on calls: a colleague can listen, with the other person's knowledge where that is appropriate, and pass you notes. What does not work remotely is distance, so if a call becomes abusive, ending it is the equivalent of stepping back.

Whatever the medium, the de-escalation elements are for safety, not for winning the call.

If you have to make a difficult call regularly, practise it on the phone with a friend, because the voice elements are harder to hear in yourself than to feel.

questions.q: What if I freeze completely in a high-stakes moment?
questions.a:
Freezing is common, and it is not a character flaw. Under sudden threat, many people's bodies stop before they act, and the moment can feel much longer than it is. The best preparation is a single physical act and a prepared sentence, rehearsed in advance, which are still available when thinking is not: a slow breath out, a step back, and something like *Give me a moment.* Rehearsal helps more than resolution, which is why the de-escalation rehearsal drill exists. If you froze once, debrief it gently, as Siobhan did with Joy, and agree what would make it easier next time, such as a code word, a clear role or a plan to leave.

It is also worth knowing that freezing often passes within seconds. A plan for those first seconds is enough.

If freezing happens often, or stays with you long after the event, it is worth talking to your GP or to an occupational health service, who can help.

watch.title: Captain Phillips: I'm the Captain Now
watch.notice: Pirates take control of a cargo ship. Watch the captain's body under extreme threat: hands visible, voice level, gaze steady, nothing sudden.

reviewPrompt: Before your next high-stakes conversation, write your expectation and one rival in a single line each, and debrief within six hours afterwards.
